title: Civil-service protections and presidential management
summary: Merit appointment, removal protection, whistleblower safeguards, and management incentives structure the President’s practical control over the federal workforce.
notes:
Civil-service law regulates the selection, retention, discipline, and management of federal personnel. The reading places those statutes alongside salary rules, financial disclosure, ethics restrictions, and partisan-balance requirements as congressional constraints on presidential personnel choices. It distinguishes employees from constitutional officers while noting that the civil service includes officials who may qualify as inferior officers.

The historical account separates three developments that are easily collapsed. The Pendleton Act of 1883 established merit-based reforms and protected workers from political-contribution coercion; it did not itself impose general cause protection for every classified worker. President McKinley’s 1897 order required just cause, written charges, notice, and an opportunity to defend. Congress subsequently enacted broader removal protection in the Lloyd–La Follette Act of 1912. The reading connects restrictions on removal of inferior officers appointed by department heads to Perkins and to Myers’s treatment of that precedent.

The Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 divided the former Civil Service Commission’s responsibilities between the Office of Personnel Management and the Merit Systems Protection Board. It strengthened management tools, created the Senior Executive Service, and protected specified employee disclosures. The competing values are practical managerial capacity, professional expertise, impartial administration, and protection against partisan retaliation. The discussion of Trump’s 2020 Schedule F order and Biden’s revocation records the textbook’s historical account; it does not resolve later changes. The editors also preserve disagreement over whether bureaucracy’s internal checks protect accountable administration or improperly resist elected priorities.
